content:
Primes, divisibility rules, HCF and LCM are quick Olympiad marks for a Class 5 student with the rules cold — and classic word-problem territory. Here is what the IMO Class 5 factors and multiples chapter tests, with a free 10-question test.

What the Class 5 Maths Olympiad Factors and Multiples chapter tests

  • Primes, composites and prime factorisation
  • Divisibility rules for 2–11
  • HCF and LCM (and HCF × LCM = product)
  • HCF/LCM word problems (bells, rods, groups)

Key facts your child should know

  • 1 is neither prime nor composite; 2 is the only even prime.
  • Digit sum ÷ 3 ⇒ number ÷ 3; last two digits ÷ 4 ⇒ number ÷ 4.
  • HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers.
  • Greatest/exact-cut → HCF; together-again/smallest-common → LCM.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Calling 1 a prime.
  • Choosing HCF when the problem needs LCM (and vice-versa).
  • Missing a prime factor in the tree.

quiz.title: IMO Class 5 Factors & Multiples Quiz
quiz.intro: Ten Olympiad-pattern questions. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: IMO Maths Olympiad Class 5: Factors and Multiples

questions.q: The number 210 is divisible by how many different prime numbers?
Find the smallest digit that can fill the blank so that 27_4 is divisible by 6.
questions.explanation: The number must be even and have a digit sum divisible by 3. With 2, the number 2724 is even and its digit sum 15 is a multiple of 3.

questions.q: Two runners complete one lap of a track in 45 seconds and 60 seconds. If they start together, after how many seconds will they meet again at the starting point?
questions.explanation: They meet at the start after a common multiple of 45 and 60 seconds; the earliest is LCM = 180 seconds.

questions.q: What is the smallest number that should be added to 4,325 so that the sum is divisible by 9?
questions.explanation: The digit sum of 4,325 is 14; the next multiple of 9 is 18, so add 4.

questions.q: What is the least number that must be subtracted from 3,000 so that the result is divisible by 7?
questions.explanation: 3,000 = 7 × 428 + 4, so removing the remainder 4 makes it divisible by 7.

questions.q: What is the smallest digit that can replace the blank so that 58_4 is divisible by 4?
questions.explanation: A number is divisible by 4 when its last two digits are. Trying digits, 5804 works because 4 ÷ 4 = 1; the smallest such digit is 0.

questions.q: Three lighthouses flash every 8, 12 and 18 seconds. If they flash together once, after how many seconds will all three flash together again?
questions.explanation: LCM of 8, 12 and 18 = 72, so all three flash together every 72 seconds.

questions.q: Find the greatest number that divides 62 and 132 leaving a remainder of 2 in each case.
questions.explanation: Subtract the remainder first: the number must divide 62 - 2 = 60 and 132 - 2 = 130 exactly. HCF(60, 130) = 10.

questions.q: Using prime factorisation, find the HCF of 60 and 105.
questions.explanation: 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 and 105 = 3 × 5 × 7. Taking each common prime the fewest times it occurs, HCF = 15.

questions.q: Three temple bells ring at intervals of 6, 8 and 12 minutes. If they ring together at 9:00 a.m., after how many minutes will they next ring together?
questions.explanation: They ring together again after the LCM of 6, 8 and 12 = 24 minutes, i.e. at 9:24 a.m.

faq.q: How do I know whether to use HCF or LCM?
faq.a: Largest piece, greatest length, exact division → HCF. Ringing together, meeting again, smallest common quantity → LCM.
Writing a number as a product of primes only, e.g. 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3.
